content: 1. A combination of discontinuing the offending drug along with skin-directed medical therapies and adjunct therapies was used to treat 21 patients across three studies. Among the 20 patients with reported outcomes (a mix of adults and children), all survived. 2. When steroids were used in children, 13 out of 15 died. In adults, the addition of steroids did not demonstrate a clear benefit when combined with drug discontinuation and/or adjunct care. Furthermore, steroids may increase the risk of opportunistic infections (OIs) and sepsis in HIV-infected patients. 3. The disease spectrum is complex, and there is limited high-quality evidence regarding the various adjunctive therapies and topical treatments, as well as their desirable and undesirable effects. Given the high potential mortality rates, the undesirable effects of the recommendations were deemed less significant. 4. Experts emphasized the importance of early detection of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). Healthcare providers should be vigilant for symptoms such as blistering, tenderness, redness, rash, erosions, and photophobia. 5. The review did not find strong evidence to support the use of oral steroids, immunoglobulins, or cyclosporine-A, which are commonly used treatments for this condition. The use of steroids may reduce survival in pediatric patients, although the evidence is of low quality. Steroids may also increase the risk of OIs and sepsis in HIV-infected individuals. 6. The costs of treatment and supportive care are expected to be very high. The recommended approach can only be implemented in larger hospitals with adequate diagnostic facilities, trained staff, good nursing care, and referral capabilities. WHO’s recommendations on nursing burn care should be followed. 7. Research gaps include the need for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to clarify the role of adjunctive therapies, such as intravenous immunoglobulin, particularly in HIV-infected populations. Other areas include the development of in vitro diagnostic methods for identifying causative medications, evaluation of high-dose oral steroids and intravenous immunoglobulins compared to best supportive care, effectiveness of different skin care dressings, and the role of infection prophylaxis in both HIV-infected and non-HIV-infected populations. 8. Dissemination and implementation of these guidelines are critical to improving the management of the included conditions. The guidelines will be distributed through WHO offices, ministries of health, collaborating centers, and other organizations, and will also be published on the WHO website. 9. Implementation will involve revising existing WHO publications and integrating the recommendations into national programs and healthcare services. This process should include participatory and consensus-driven adaptation to local needs, with modifications limited to weak recommendations and justified transparently. 10. An enabling environment should be created to support evidence-based practices, including changes in healthcare practitioners’ behavior. Local professional societies may play a key role in this process. 11. Program managers should integrate these guidelines into existing HIV, dermatological, and general healthcare programs. This integration should be planned to gradually incorporate the recommendations into routine practices. 12. Essential medicines recommended in this document are included in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines. Program managers should ensure that adequate quantities of these drugs in the recommended dosages are available through existing health system supply chains. 13. Training for healthcare workers is essential to improve the diagnosis and recognition of skin disorders, particularly as these conditions may present differently in individuals with varying skin colors. Training can be integrated with ongoing capacity-building in HIV care. 14. Laboratory services are a critical component of HIV care. Diagnosing skin conditions associated with HIV may require laboratory investigations, such as skin scrapings, biopsies, and gram stains. Updated training and additional supplies may be necessary for laboratory personnel. 15. Monitoring and evaluation should be incorporated into the implementation process to assess the impact of the guidelines on care quality. Data collection on opportunistic conditions and related outcomes should be prioritized, even if these conditions are not included in national HIV core indicators. 16. The ultimate goal of these guidelines is to improve the management of skin and oral HIV-associated conditions in children and adults. Their successful implementation depends on well-planned, participatory processes and integration into national healthcare systems.
